claims: A market is an arrangement bringing buyers and sellers into contact to exchange a product or resource.
A market need not be a single physical place because buyers and sellers can communicate and agree exchange at a distance.
Physical and digital markets differ in how buyers and sellers make contact and arrange transactions.
The same seller can use both physical and digital channels, whose usefulness depends on access, information and fulfilment.
A physical market involves buyers and sellers meeting at a physical location to arrange exchange.
Physical contact can allow direct inspection but may require travel and attendance during opening times.
A digital market uses electronic communication to bring buyers and sellers into contact and arrange exchange.
Digital contact can extend reach but depends on access, reliable information and suitable arrangements for payment and delivery.

CU-6145-3.1:
A market is an arrangement bringing buyers and sellers into contact to exchange a product or resource. Buyers seek something they want and sellers offer it on terms they are willing to consider. Contact allows information about the product, quantity and payment to pass between them. The arrangement can exist without a sale being completed in every conversation: potential buyers may compare offers or decide not to buy. What matters is the connection through which exchange can be arranged.

A market is therefore broader than a building or a row of stalls. A vegetable stall is one familiar example, but a repair service booked remotely can also participate in a market. Markets can concern goods, services or resources such as labour. In each case identify what is being exchanged and who occupies each side. A person looking for paid work offers labour services, while an employer seeks those services. Saying that someone is a buyer in one transaction does not mean they cannot be a seller in another. The same household may buy groceries and supply labour.

Physical and digital describe ways of bringing buyers and sellers together. In a physical arrangement, customers can visit a location and discuss a product in person. In a digital arrangement, electronic communication can let customers view offers and place orders at a distance. These channels can overlap. An invented tailor might take measurements at a shop, show available fabrics through an online catalogue and confirm collection electronically. That combination does not create three separate products or require three separate sellers. It shows different stages of one trading arrangement.

To classify a case, inspect how contact and ordering occur rather than the payment method alone. A customer using a bank card at a physical stall has not thereby turned the stall into a digital marketplace. Conversely, an online order collected and paid for in cash still used digital contact to arrange the sale. Payment, communication and delivery are related parts of a transaction, but they answer different questions. A successful channel must make exchange workable for the relevant people: attractive pictures are insufficient if customers cannot obtain accurate information or receive the goods.

An invented seller of handmade bags could reach local passers-by at a stall and distant customers through electronic orders. Direct inspection may matter when customers want to check stitching. Distance ordering may matter when travelling to the stall is difficult. Neither channel is automatically cheaper or better: travel, operating hours, access, delivery and confidence affect the comparison. This links to exchange in topic 2.3 and introduces the buyer and seller decisions analysed in market forces in topic 3.2. First establish the market arrangement; then explain how the relevant information and constraints influence exchange. A market description should name the product and the people connected. A building with no arrangement for buyer-seller exchange is not established as a market merely because people gather there.
CU-6145-3.1.2:
A physical market involves buyers and sellers meeting at a physical location to arrange exchange. The location may contain several traders or a single seller. The defining point is direct physical contact through the trading arrangement, rather than whether the place is indoors, formal or large. An invented furniture showroom can be a physical trading location, just as a small produce stall can. The product need not be paid for immediately to make the arrangement relevant: a buyer can inspect, compare and agree a later collection.

Direct inspection can reduce uncertainty about qualities such as size, finish or freshness. Face-to-face discussion may help a buyer describe a repair problem or ask questions. These benefits have costs and limits. Travelling requires time and possibly money. Trading may be limited to opening hours, and the seller reaches people able to attend. Seeing a product does not remove every uncertainty about its later performance. A sensible explanation links the case fact to the benefit: inspecting a chair can help a buyer judge its dimensions, while inspecting a sealed package may reveal much less about what is inside. Do not assume that a physical location assures quality or honesty.

A digital market uses electronic communication to bring buyers and sellers into contact and arrange exchange. A customer may read a product description, compare offers and place an order without visiting the seller first. The product itself can still be physical. For an invented pottery business, digital orders might connect customers in another town with bowls made in its local workshop. Describing the contact as digital does not imply that the bowls travel electronically or that transport is unnecessary.

Distance contact can extend reach and reduce a buyer's need to travel before ordering. It depends on customers having suitable access and being able to judge the information supplied. Photographs may not show exact colour or scale, so dimensions and clear descriptions matter. Delivery, collection and payment must also be workable. A failed connection or unclear collection arrangement can prevent a potential contact from becoming a completed exchange. These practical requirements make comparison conditional. Digital contact may suit customers who already know the product, while first-time buyers may prefer direct inspection. Neither preference establishes that the other channel has no market role.

A seller can combine digital enquiries with physical inspection or collection. The economic question is whether the arrangement connects the relevant buyers and sellers effectively. Compare what each group needs to know, what access it has and how exchange can be completed. This links the two market types back to the general definition: a building is one possible meeting point, while communication at a distance can provide another arrangement for contact. A contact channel can be useful even when a particular buyer chooses not to purchase. Availability for exchange and completion of a sale are different observations; the definition concerns the arrangement that makes trading possible.

The invented Pebble Pots business sells at a weekend stall. Customers can inspect pots, but distant customers cannot attend regularly. It proposes an electronic catalogue with ordering and shop collection; some customers lack reliable internet. (a) Describe three features of the proposed market arrangement (6). (b) Examine how it may affect contact between buyers and seller (7). (c) Suggest a suitable combination of channels (7).

(a) The stall is a physical point for meeting and inspection. The catalogue offers electronic information and ordering at a distance. Collection remains physical, so the business combines channels. (b) Distant buyers can enquire and order without a first journey, extending potential contact. Clear sizes and descriptions become more important because remote buyers cannot directly inspect before ordering. Customers without reliable internet may struggle to use the catalogue, and collection still requires travel. (c) Retain the stall while adding a clear catalogue and agreed collection arrangements. This preserves access for customers without internet and inspection for uncertain buyers. Provide dimensions and allow questions to reduce remote uncertainty. The judgement depends on whether the extra contact can be served reliably; catalogue views alone are not completed exchanges.

Context: Pebble Pots. Parts/allocation: (a) physical stall, remote catalogue, mixed fulfilment, 2 each = 6. (b) reach mechanism 3, information issue 2, access/collection constraints 2 = 7. (c) combined proposal 2, inspection/inclusion reasons 3, feasibility judgement 2 = 7.

(a) Arrangement connecting buyers and sellers for exchange. (b) Communication can connect them remotely, so a shared physical place is unnecessary. (c) Electronic describes contact, while the goods can be delivered or collected physically. (d) Payment method differs from how buyer and seller meet. (e) Inspection reveals relevant visible qualities, reducing uncertainty. (f) Travel/opening hours can restrict attendance. (g) Reliable access allows customers to receive information and place orders. (h) Remote ordering can be followed by physical inspection or collection.

Parts/allocation: eight at 2 each. Precision: (a) contact + exchange; (b) remote communication + no shared place; (c) contact method + physical fulfilment; (d) payment/contact distinction with stall application; (e) visible information + reduced uncertainty; (f) travel/hours + access effect; (g) reliable access + effective contact; (h) electronic stage + physical stage.

The invented Horizon Chairs seller has a showroom where buyers inspect chairs. It considers closing it and accepting electronic orders with delivery. Buyers frequently ask about size and comfort; many live far away, while some lack electronic access. No evidence about comparative costs is available. (a) Define a physical market (2). (b) Explain two benefits of digital contact for this seller (4). (c) Explain how closure could affect buyers' ability to arrange satisfactory exchange (7). (d) Discuss whether the showroom should be replaced completely (7).

(a) Market in which buyers and sellers meet at a physical location to arrange exchange. (b) Distant customers can enquire without an initial journey. Electronic descriptions can be consulted outside a showroom visit, widening opportunities for contact. (c) Closure removes direct inspection, making size information and descriptions more important. Comfort is difficult to judge remotely, potentially leaving buyers uncertain. Customers lacking access may lose a practical contact channel. Delivery can make receipt possible for distant buyers, but does not itself solve the information problem. (d) Digital contact has a strong distance-access benefit, but replacement risks excluding some buyers and losing inspection. With no comparative cost data, do not claim closure is cheaper. Retain some inspection opportunity while testing remote ordering and reliable delivery; complete replacement is more defensible if access and information needs can be met satisfactorily.

Context: Horizon Chairs. Parts/allocation: (a) market contact 1, physical location 1. (b) two contact benefits with buyer effects, 2 each = 4. (c) inspection/information mechanism 3, electronic exclusion 2, delivery distinction 2 = 7. (d) distance benefit 2, inspection/access limits 2, conditional judgement avoiding invented cost superiority 3 = 7.
essay_plan

Evaluate whether an invented school-uniform repair service should accept digital orders alongside a weekly physical collection point when families have different access and some repairs need inspection (9).

For: electronic contact can let families describe work and arrange a collection without repeated visits. A physical point retains inspection where the repair is uncertain and gives access to families who cannot order electronically. Against: coordinating the two channels may create confusion if the information or collection arrangements differ. Remote descriptions can be incomplete, and the physical point still requires attendance. Judgement: combine the channels if clear information and a workable collection routine make the service accessible. Keep inspection for uncertain repairs rather than treating a message as sufficient evidence for every job. The decisive condition is effective contact and fulfilment for the relevant families, not the mere presence of an electronic catalogue.

Argument for: complementary access/inspection effects, up to 4. Argument against: coordination, information and attendance limitations developed, up to 4. Judgement: condition-based workable routine, 1. Total 9.
